speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These borrowers often need short-term credit urgently, but cannot obtain it from financial institutions, possibly due to their level of income or credit history.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In regulating licensed moneylenders, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) seeks to maintain a balance in allowing individual borrowers reasonable access to credit from licensed sources, while ensuring that borrowers, particularly lower-income borrowers, are adequately protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Advisory Committee on Moneylending (ACML) was convened in June 2014 to comprehensively review the regulatory regime for moneylending with these objectives in mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Committee issued its Final Report in May 2015 with 15 recommendations to MinLaw.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2015, we introduced stricter caps on borrowing costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In March 2016, we launched the Moneylenders Credit Bureau (MLCB), which facilitates better tracking and monitoring of unsecured loans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: MLCB provides up-to-date details of a borrower's creditworthiness and indebtedness, to enable moneylenders to make a more informed and responsible lending decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Moneylenders (Amendment) Bill is the latest step in these efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Its key objectives are to: (a) provide better protection for borrowers; (b) strengthen the regulation of moneylenders; and (c) professionalise the moneylending industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: One key change introduced by clause 19 in this Bill is the aggregate loan cap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Moneylenders Rules presently cap the amount of unsecured credit an individual may borrow from any single moneylender.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, there are borrowers who approach multiple moneylenders for loans and, consequently, may still become over-indebted despite the current restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The proposed aggregate loan cap in the Bill addresses this issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The aggregate loan cap is intended as a measure to prevent over-borrowing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Even though only a small number of Singaporeans over-borrow today, they still need help with managing their debt.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We also want to ensure that the numbers do not grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: MinLaw will work with VWOs and the moneylending industry to help such borrowers improve their situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Moneylenders Association of Singapore (MLAS) is also developing a more formalised framework, the Moneylenders Debt Restructuring Scheme, to complement existing debt assistance schemes run by VWOs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Details of this industry-led initiative will be announced by MLAS later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To facilitate the implementation of the aggregate loan cap, clause 18 of the Bill introduces a new Part IIIA, which sets out the regulatory framework for MLCB, and imposes new obligations on moneylenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Moneylenders will also be required to submit accurate borrower information to MLCB and provide timely updates to MLCB when borrowers repay their loans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Likewise, the Bill requires MLCB to facilitate moneylenders’ requests for credit reports.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also requires MLCB to protect the integrity, security and confidentiality of any borrower information and credit reports in its possession, in addition to existing protections under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) 2012.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill introduces new provisions to allow the Registrar of Moneylenders (the Registrar) to exercise greater oversight on MLCB.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, the proposed section 30F will enable the Registrar to replace the MLCB operator under specific conditions, such as if the operator fails to satisfy its obligations under the Moneylenders Act, and the proposed section 30I gives the Registrar various powers to ensure the smooth and continued operation of MLCB, especially in the event of a handover to another operator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Together, these amendments provide a stronger regulatory framework to provide individual borrowers with safer access to personal credit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Next, the Bill also seeks to strengthen the regulation of the moneylending industry in three ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, Part II of the Moneylenders Act empowers the Registrar to revoke, suspend, refuse to issue, or refuse to renew a moneylenders’ licence on a number of grounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Specifically, sections 7(d) to (g) permit the Registrar to do so where he is not satisfied as to the qualification, experience or character of an individual applicant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is also applicable to a director, partner or substantial shareholder of a corporate applicant, or a person responsible for the management of the moneylending business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill expands the scope of this power to include persons who are presently employed or engaged, or whom a moneylender proposes to employ or engage, to assist in the business of moneylending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 10 also introduces a new section 11A, which provides that a moneylender must obtain the Registrar’s written approval before employing or engaging any assistant in its business of moneylending.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, the Act requires that a moneylender obtain the Registrar’s approval as soon as practicable after someone has become a substantial shareholder or changes his substantial shareholding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 11 of the Bill will require moneylenders to obtain this approval before the person becomes a substantial shareholder, or before any shareholder increases his substantial shareholding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Existing approvals to engage in moneylending may be revoked if the Registrar discovers that any employee, director or substantial shareholder of the moneylender is not a fit and proper person or a person of good character.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Failure to comply will also lead to enforcement and licensing action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This will ensure that moneylenders holding licences today but who are not actively operating a moneylending business do not retain these licences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Thirdly, the Bill will also strengthen the regulation of moneylenders by tightening the mandatory requirements on loan terms and contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, it is an offence for a moneylender to make any loan contract that does not truly state the principal or interest rate of the loan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 12 expands the scope of this offence to include loan contracts that do not truly state the late interest rate or any permitted fees payable as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the current regime, borrowers are protected from onerous loan terms by existing caps on fees, interest and late interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If a loan transaction is found by the Court to have breached these caps, the Court can reopen the transaction and the borrower may be relieved from excessive payments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, it is currently not an offence if a moneylender breaches these caps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is changed by clauses 13 and 14 of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The third area which the Bill touches on is the professionalisation of the moneylending industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill introduces a new section 6A, which requires that all licensed moneylenders be companies with a minimum paid-up capital of not less than the prescribed amount.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Today, nearly 70% of licensed moneylenders have already registered as companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 17 of the Bill will also impose a new requirement on every moneylender to submit annual audited accounts to the Registrar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Audit requirements are not unusual and are presently imposed on many regulated entities across various sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Given the nature of the moneylending business, there is greater imperative for independent audit supervision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Going forward, MinLaw will complement these regulatory reforms with business-led initiatives to further professionalise the moneylending industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We seek to encourage good business practices and better business models that can benefit borrowers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These include more effective methods of credit assessment to reduce default rates, more compassionate and responsive debt assistance schemes and more affordable terms of credit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: To encourage new business models, promulgate better business practices and spur improvements, MinLaw will explore lifting the current moratorium in a limited and controlled fashion, to allow a few new players with established track records in related financial areas to pilot new business models in the moneylending industry.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many seek moneylenders over the banks because of their ease and convenience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some do not qualify for bank loans and, therefore, resort to moneylending services for short-term credit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These people are often vulnerable and every effort must be taken to ensure that they know what they are getting themselves into.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Education is timely, and counselling in the management of finances is perhaps important as the total outstanding amount in licensed moneylending and the number of borrowers is on the rise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although the proposed regulations will protect low-income families and prevent them from borrowing beyond their means, I wonder if our efforts to regulate the industry may also inadvertently push some of these borrowers into the outstretched arms of illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This may lead to another set of issues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a Member of Parliament (MP), I am sure many of us in this House have met families who have borrowed from illegal moneylenders and have their lives turned upside down.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my own town and our effort to drive home the message against illegal moneylending, our own branch office became a target of intimidation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As for licensed moneylenders, many of us have also come across a growing number of residents who are facing problems with their repayments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Paying the principal amount borrowed, together with the interest, is enough to break many.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the new loan cap to protect borrowers, especially from licensed moneylenders, is, of course, a welcome one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will not have a situation where Moneylender A will not know that Moneylender B is loaning the same amount to the same family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The move to obtain credit reports before issuing a loan is perhaps long overdue, and this, taken in tandem with the measures undertaken by banks and credit card companies, will be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MLCB will act perhaps like a goalkeeper and verify lenders’ loan statuses before a loan is granted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But will the imposition of a nominal fee for the checking of records put off moneylenders from exercising due diligence, no matter how small the amount may be?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What if they do not check the records and continue to issue loans more than the cap that is stipulated within the Act?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the Registrar have the necessary powers to enforce that moneylenders fall in line and that they will have the power to take punitive and deterrent action against such errant moneylenders?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The call for regulation in this Bill is timely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Seeking the Registrar’s approval before employing assistants will enhance professionalism in the industry.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the Registrar also have the powers to get them to fall in line?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Accountability and transparency are the keywords of the amendments tabled in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But are those who are borrowing aware of the costs involved and consequences of getting a loan from the moneylenders?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the moneylenders be required to advise them accordingly and will the Registrar ensure that they do?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As stated earlier, educating vulnerable groups, especially low-income families, of the pitfalls of failure to repay loans to moneylenders, is important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The "O$P$" signs that were, perhaps, more common in the past, are fast becoming a thing of the past.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we still read of isolated cases of paint being splashed on doors and debtors being intimidated and even other debtors being forced to become runners for illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must not be complacent in our Home Team efforts to crack down on illegal moneylending but it is also important that we regulate the legal and licensed moneylender industry to prevent any abuse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would perhaps be educational for Members present in this House if the Senior Minister of State could share with us if any studies have been conducted to ascertain the reasons as to why people borrow from moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the causes and what are the costs?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the average amount borrowed and the interest rates levied?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are those interest rates explained to the borrower and are those rates acceptable to the borrower?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because many of them take loans perhaps in desperate situations and agree to almost everything under the sun.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I tend to agree with the counselling part.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But Government-administered lending is something I am not comfortable with.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The onus is on the borrower to exercise due diligence and to ascertain if the loan required is necessary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if it is, will it be possible for them to repay the sum within the stipulated period?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is where the Government can perhaps lend a hand by making available counsellors who would advise people in need of their options.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps a dedicated unit within the Registry would go a long way in advising people who would like to seek the services of a moneylender.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My last clarification has to do with debt recovery.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to ask the Ministry if there are acceptable standards of debt recovery that are set and how they are being policed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have come across feedback that there are sometimes methods that border on criminal intimidation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the amendments proposed in the Bill aim to protect borrowers from over-borrowing and predatory moneylending practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am concerned the Government might be over-tightening the rules, making credit so inaccessible to individual borrowers that they are driven by desperation to unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The main thrust of my speech is to ask that the Senior Minister of State allay this concern through the explanation of specific reasons and facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This appears to be an achievement of tough enforcement combined with the licensing and regulation of legalised moneylending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But just as loan sharking and illegal moneylending cases are declining to new lows, the Ministry set up an Advisory Committee on Moneylending to review the regulations and make recommendations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most significant changes were borrowing caps based on income, caps on interest rates and fees and standardised loan contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In principle, it is good for the Government to review regulations after a period of their operation to see what can be done better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is also a worry that the Ministry could be fixing something that is not broken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, this something is not just not broken, it is working very well in tandem with strict enforcement against unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Senior Minister of State three questions to allay this worry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, while the logic of the tightening, such as pegging borrowing caps to income and caps on interest rates and fees, is hard to disagree with, it is also important that we look at hard data for evidence-based policymaking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister please share with the House the number of unlicensed moneylending cases reported and the number of offenders arrested in 2016 and 2017?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These numbers could tell us whether the 2015 tightening had the effect of pushing more borrowers to unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, the proposed Bill will empower MinLaw to go further than the 2015 tightening, allowing the Ministry to set up an aggregate loan cap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the 2015 tightening, borrowers could borrow up to the loan cap from each moneylender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the further tightening allowed by the new regulatory framework, borrowers could borrow up to the loan cap from all moneylenders combined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is quite a drastic tightening of credit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State please inform the House what are the new developments on borrowing, new data on moneylending trends that have led to this escalated tightening?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third question follows from the first and the second questions, and is concerned with the balance of things, between protecting borrowers from over-borrowing and driving them to turn to unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State please advise whether the Ministry has studied the probability that this further tightening would drive borrowers to turn to unlicensed moneylenders, and whether the Ministry has the monitoring tools to measure this possible effect?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, other than the main points above, I have four other minor points to raise for the Senior Minister of State to address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, in the 2015 adoption of the Advisory Committee report, two of the recommendations were put on hold to be reviewed later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are (a) the lifting of the moratorium on granting of new licences so as to encourage competition and bring down interest rates; and (b) the creation of guidelines for debt-collecting practices so as to further professionalise the industry and distinguish it from unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they have not been reviewed, whether she thinks it is timely to review them now, given the extensive makeover to prevent over-borrowing and to professionalise the industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, one of the recommendations in the Advisory Committee report was that, while no recommendations were made in respect to the location of moneylenders in the heartland, the Committee advised that the Registry should monitor the situation and ensure that it is not aggravated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A research policy report published by the Centre of Banking and Finance Law at the Faculty of Law, National University of Singapore, in July 2015, shows that more than half of the licensed moneylenders were located in primarily residential areas rather than the commercial areas of town centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be a case for the Ministry to commission a study using current geographical methods to determine whether location matters in encouraging unnecessary and excessive borrowing and thus whether or not the location of moneylenders should be regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, would the Ministry look into working with the moneylending industry towards standardising loan products, with guidelines to advertise these products at their premises in a transparent manner?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will further professionalise the industry as well as better fulfil the 2015 recommendation to standardise loan contracts and practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are some interesting peer-to-peer (P2P) lending startups in Singapore, such as Funding Societies from Indonesia and the local outfit MoolahSense, linking up individual investors with small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As far as I know, there are no platforms, legal or otherwise, that are connecting individual borrowers with lenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are risks associated with these potentially disruptive fintech innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, many individual borrowers could be borrowing from licensed moneylenders because they are shut out from mainstream credit facilities and need loans to manage their cash flow problems in their micro-enterprise business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, as I mentioned at the start of my speech, I support the aim of this Bill to protect borrowers from over-borrowing and from predatory moneylending practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would greatly upset the balance between giving borrowers credit access and clamping down on loan sharks that has been hard won.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister of State would allay this concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And with this caution, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Due to its unique nature, moneylending is relatively costly for credit provision, if you think about it, especially when lending to individual small borrowers with low incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We need to also understand many small-time borrowers are often caught in a desperate situation for funds and thus are vulnerable to exploitation by some moneylenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But beyond this, does the Ministry also know that moneylending is actually a very small part of the consumer credit market?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, let us put that into perspective In planning our handling of the issues related to moneylending, I feel it is important to maintain a well-balanced approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Whatever penalty regimen we are administering, we must bear in mind the spectrum of persons on the moneylending “food chain”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In this sense, it is a welcome move to have the limits set as prescribed in this Bill and I support that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also stated that MLCB will check if borrowers have exceeded the limits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, a licensed moneylender saw me and shared this anecdote.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have informed the person of my sharing this in my speech today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Two Permanent Residents (PRs) borrowed money from this moneylender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They had their identity cards and passed the usual checks that needed to be carried out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, when it came to repayment, they did not comply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, as is usually done, the moneylenders will send debt collectors to their homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The person who opened the door told the debt collector that the two guys who were PRs have never lived there and they were just using the address.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, he went on to say that he, as a Singapore Citizen, had allowed the two men to use his name in support of their PR applications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: He further elaborated to the debt collector that the two men had a track record of borrowing and then not being traceable and many had come to the house before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, he felt that this moneylending company will never get the money back.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The moneylender made a Police report giving all details present and available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, the response from the Police came back that they had treated the case as closed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Being a bit disappointed, the moneylender came to see me and, of course, made some representation, confided that it was not really about just getting back the money but more that it was the duty to highlight to the authorities that these two men were going around and cheating and still circulating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We also need to know to prevent or reduce incidents like this in the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We also do not want a situation whereby the tightening of rules is seen to force genuine moneylenders to exit the market and loan sharks to take over dominance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, moneylenders can also tend to be at the mercy of some borrowers, who declare bankrupt readily when unable to repay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In this Bill, it is also stated after dispensing the loans, moneylenders must update MLCB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What if some people borrow from multiple lenders?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, it is a combination of borrowing from both licensed and unlicensed lenders to date.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As long as parties comply and play by the rules, the moneylending industry can enhance its image and professionalism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Many people are looking to help regulate this area already.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Work has been done by MinLaw and by ACML.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One other group we need to nurture and train includes mediators as well who can help in this industry, as mediation cases may tend to increase between the borrower and the lenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The challenge is how to create and have a moneylending system that recognises the need to adequately protect the vulnerable borrowers from the exploitative actions of some, whilst ensuring ongoing access to credit by people who really and truly have no access to alternatives and may then be tempted to enter the unsavoury world of illegal lending.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that going to borrow money is the only solution for some, albeit this is often a flawed one, because servicing the loan would sink the borrower deeper into the red.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The slope is a slippery one: easy to fall into and hard to get out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, I support the introduction of a cap on loans from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It will hopefully prevent some people from borrowing way beyond their means.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moneylending is a problem that has lingered for some time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A few years ago, I spoke about the loanshark problem and illegal moneylending in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thanks to the Government's intervention and the great effort of the Police, loansharking activities appear to have abated somewhat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But there will also be the issue of people needing to borrow money and then over-borrowing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My only concern is whether this new cap will lead to even more underground moneylending activities and at even more cut-throat rates for desperate borrowers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government enhance the penalties for anyone caught operating an illegal moneylending joint?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will those reaching the cap be asked to attend credit counselling?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have to nip the problem in the bud.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why are people getting into debt in the first place?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These days, it is also very common to come across advertisements for "$0" upfront products.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, when you calculate the cost of the product as advertised upfront and the total sum of the instalments, there is a significant disparity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One could purchase several expensive items without forking out a cent, only to realise months down the road that he or she is being saddled with bills that they cannot pay off.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should there be some restrictions on the way advertisements for hire purchases are presented?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Credit card debt is a serious problem in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The convenience of online shopping probably contributes to this trend.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Gambling addicts are another group of vulnerable people who often get caught in the never-ending spiral of borrowing and owing money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In light of the trends above, will the Ministry consider a widespread campaign about financial management and prudence, perhaps more education?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would suggest that it start as early as upper primary school.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should ingrain in our young minds to spend within their means as well as the ill of gambling because gambling is just like drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The moment they start to gamble, it can be addictive and difficult to get it off.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also have seen young graduates use credit card overdraft facilities in order to support their lifestyle which they cannot afford.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More awareness also needs to be drawn to the Credit Counselling Singapore programme, which aims to help individuals in debt through education, counselling and debt management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Limiting the loan amount that the moneylenders can lend is a good thing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am concerned that those who are desperate for money may turn to "ah longs", or loan sharks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government should pay attention to this trend and increase the penalty for "ah longs".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should also reflect why some people are mired in debts.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nowadays, zero downpayment instalment plans and the convenience of online shopping have tempted many consumers to overspend.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Statistics have also shown that there are more and more Singaporeans owing credit card debts and more people are seeking help for gambling addiction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I hope the Government can step up education on financial prudence and management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To address this issue, I think we should start from schools, even beginning from primary schools.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should let students know the ills of gambling and that they should never start on it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because once you start gambling, you will be addicted and it is very difficult to get out of, just like drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, we should also let every Singaporean know the importance of spending within his/her means.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe this is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Very often, the interest rates charged by moneylenders are already so high that borrowers struggle to repay one loan and then goes to more moneylenders to borrow to repay the initial loan, thus setting in motion a vicious circle ending in more financial trouble and possible bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I am also afraid that the proposed rules may cause borrowers to turn to unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, it is very difficult to prevent collaboration between licensed and unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, a licensed moneylender possessing the contact details of a borrower could pass the contact information to unlicensed moneylenders, who may subsequently send messages promoting their easy loans.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most of the time, the recipients do not even know that these messages come from illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some residents have given me feedback that they receive a lot of unsolicited short message service (SMS) messages about such unsecured loans after they have approached legal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, an alarming aspect is that some of the borrowers think that these messages come from licensed moneylenders and are well regulated when, in fact, they are not.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to know if the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is working with the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) for mobile operators to disable any subscriber identity module (SIM) cards which are used by illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the authorities can take into account the suggestions I have made.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that the Government has strengthened our laws to ensure stricter controls and measures towards those who lend money and seek to reclaim their monies, as well as to ensure safety for those who borrow money.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As MPs in this House, many of us would have heard from residents their laments about harassment from loansharks and even licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the Government's move to strengthen our Moneylenders Act through this amendment Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To elaborate, I strongly support the insertion of section 11(A)(10).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to keep track of and monitor every employee or person who works for a company that lends money or an entity whose core business is moneylending.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been instances where moneylending companies have painted themselves to be run by thugs no different from loanshark syndicates.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met residents who have shared their nasty experience where the moneylender assistants or debt collectors from moneylending companies had acted aggressively when dealing with clients in debt collection, with threats and vulgarities hurled at the debtors when the debt could not be paid up immediately or in full as demanded.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As moneylending companies are registered companies and the assistants or debt collectors are employees of these registered companies, there must be some form of decorum and sense of responsibility and respect in carrying out their duties, even that of debt collection, in addition to having good moral character with no prior criminal records.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These assistants or debt collectors who are employees of the moneylending companies must be trained, monitored and disciplined in the ethics of debt collection, not through aggression but by being firm yet respectful in retrieving the debts owed to the company.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, how do the moneylending companies, the Government or even employers monitor borrowers' record of borrowing, especially those of the employees?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the banks, there is the Credit Bureau Report that monitors borrowers' credit and record of borrowing, which can be accessed and shared by the banks and with employers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we ensure the borrowers themselves do not over-extend through borrowing excessively from different licensed moneylenders?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How much borrower information is collected and shared?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fact that this is a private company designated as a credit bureau, the issue of confidentiality and privacy is a concern for borrowers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be a sharing of such credit information of these borrowers among the different moneylending companies?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On what platforms would such information be shared?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will such information be available under the Credit Bureau Report or made available to the banks or employers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to the Ministry's clarifications on these questions I raised.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my concerns and questions, I support the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have a few points to clarify on the wide-ranging powers and sensitive personal data that the Registrar and the Moneylenders Credit Bureau will possess, and the other methods for promoting responsible and safe lending.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this is sound in principle, can I find out how enforcement of these provisions will look like in practice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry verify whether the individual has carried out any such moneylending businesses overseas?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to work with foreign authorities?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Registrar will have wide discretion to refuse or cancel approval granted for various applications under the amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Registrar be providing reasons for refusing applications?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the channels and grounds for appeal for someone whose application has been refused or cancelled?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that licensees and MLCB will possess sensitive borrowers' information, I am concerned about the security and confidentiality of the data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would there not be similar, if not greater, need for oversight over individual licensees who may not have the same technical ability as MLCB in maintaining security arrangements?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the same note, will the Ministry be providing technical guidance to support licensees in protecting these sensitive data?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, can the Minister also clarify what duties a public agency that obtains borrowers' information and data under section 30ZC are under to protect that information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, public agencies are subject to relevant internal Government rules and sector-specific legislation as stated in the PDPC’s website frequently asked questions (FAQ).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are these specific rules and duties public agencies are bound by when they obtain borrowers' information and data under section 30ZC, to protect that information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the disclosure of information is only permissible for policy formulation or review, would it be necessary for the personal data to be in an individually identifiable form?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it not be sufficient for the purposes of formulating broad policy for the data to be anonymised?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, in response to a call for feedback over Facebook, Mr Kane Tan highlighted the concern of moneylender advertising.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, moneylender advertising is regulated under directions issued by the Registrar of Moneylenders, in addition to general requirements for all advertisements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, loan-shark advertisements through SMS messages remain common.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have plans to step up efforts to clamp down on such illegal advertising and to help the layperson distinguish between licensed and unlicensed moneylenders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such efforts must be appropriately targeted, recognising that those who turn to loan sharks may have lower literacy skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Awareness-raising must also dispel the false belief that only those who are involved in illegal activities like gambling or drugs turn to loan sharks when, in fact, "ordinary" people from all walks of life can be entangled with illegal moneylending.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the Minister clarify whether platforms that are not themselves moneylenders but connect people to other moneylenders are covered under the Registrar’s direction on advertising?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, can a search aggregator that compares moneylenders advertise through sponsored links or online advertisements which are not permitted for licensees themselves?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Allowing such advertising would seem to circumvent the objectives of regulating moneylender advertisements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have a timeline for the review of these recommendations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, to complement its efforts in regulating the supply-side of borrowing, it is also important for the Government to address the demand for credit by providing support for vulnerable borrowers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are two dimensions to this problem – preventing individuals from getting into problem debt in the first place and helping those who are in debt to regain control of their finances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Credit Counselling Singapore is a debt charity that has done commendable work through counselling, facilitating debt restructuring and education on credit management.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to increase its support for and promote the work of such organisations to provide individuals with alternatives to illegal moneylending.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the annual increases in the total outstanding loans taken with licensed moneylenders have been substantial.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, does the Ministry have statistics on what purposes such loans were for, such as setting up new businesses, family emergencies or to feed gambling habits?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hopefully, with this cap and public education, people will learn to manage their finances better and their need to borrow can be curbed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need more measures to boost financial management education.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such public education programmes should start young and, for older persons, they should be customised, even in dialects, in order to be more effective and reach a wider range of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Going forward, moneylenders will have to obtain online credit reports from MLCB before issuing a loan.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The timing of the input of data affects the total borrowing that lenders will rely on for their approval of loans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Any lead time will create opportunities for system arbitrage and leakages.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I am concerned − as was also expressed by other Members in the House − that with the tightening of regulations, desperate borrowers will be compelled to resort to illegal moneylenders.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How effectively we can curtail illegal moneylenders remains challenging, especially with harassment cases, including physical and verbal threats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry review whether current penalties prove to be sufficient deterrents and whether punishments, especially physical ones, such as caning, need to be increased?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is that a borrower may try to circumvent the regulations by falsifying income documents or resort to reporting a higher income to meet the loan criteria.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures does the Ministry have to prevent such cases?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the level of household debt remains high, the level of unsecured debt with loans taken from banks, while it had caused some concern two years ago, the Credit Limit Management Measures by MAS have reversed this trend.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendments proposed under this Bill will enhance these measures as moneylending is further tightened.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Easy accessibility to finances can feed unnecessary expenditures and habits, such as gambling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed measures will prevent such borrowing from spiralling out of control.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is good that the number of high debtors with banks is decreasing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we must be cautious that the borrowing has not been channelled elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Debtors facing caps imposed on loans from banks − and soon from licensed moneylenders − might turn to unlicensed lenders, such as loan sharks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This means that the authorities must keep an even closer watch on unlicensed moneylenders who resort to creative tactics, such as sending WhatsApp messages using overseas numbers to lure borrowers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tightly linked to the accessibility of easy loans is their perceived attractiveness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even though these moneylenders are restricted in terms of the channels they can use to advertise, they often have glitzy websites that do not provide upfront information on the interest rates for loans or the total amount of interest that needs to be paid for the full term of the loan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, while most moneylenders follow the rules, there are some that have resorted to unscrupulous means to take advantage of borrowers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the top two types of complaints, and will the Registry consider publishing a list of blacklisted companies and a brief description of the complaint, so that borrowers are kept informed on the issues that they need to be aware of?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently there is a list of suspended companies at the end of the list of registered moneylenders, but it is easy to miss the names as one would have to scroll to the end of 159 companies to see them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Registry consider making the list of suspended moneylenders more accessible, informative and prominent?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In terms of educating the public, will the Ministry conduct roadshows and other outreach programmes to educate the public on the law on moneylending and how to differentiate between a legal and illegal moneylender, and on the ills of borrowing in general?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every day in the heartlands, one would encounter many banks promoting various credit facilities and walk past the premises of many moneylending companies that have mushroomed in our town centres and malls.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it is difficult to find educational posters or information sources on the ills of irresponsible money borrowing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry consider finding ways to balance this exposure to moneylending sources with educational information on the downsides of being burdened with debt?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While it is true that a borrower will overcome any physical distance to seek loans and that such access can be attained online, limiting the immediacy of access and physical presence of these companies can reduce the temptation and convenience of borrowing in general.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the above, this Bill will further help prevent reckless borrowing and reduce default rates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will now respond to the queries raised by the Members, which fall under several broad themes: (a) borrower protection and public education; (b) unlicensed moneylending; (c) advertising by moneylenders; (d) usage and protection of borrowers’ confidential data; (e) operationalising and enforcing the provisions of the Bill; and (f) the recommendations of ACML.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will address each of these in turn.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some Members have raised concerns about whether the aggregate loan cap will drive borrowers to borrow from unlicensed moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about the moneylending trends which have led to the introduction of this aggregate loan cap.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As explained in my speech, the cap was a recommendation of ACML in 2015 and has been calibrated to achieve a balance between protecting borrowers and preserving reasonable access to credit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since the recommendation was made, we have observed an upward trend in the amount of outstanding debt owed by moneylending borrowers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not a big number, around 610 borrowers, but the aggregate cap will help us to nip the over-borrowing in the bud before it gets worse.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh had also asked for 2017 statistics on the number of borrowers and the amount of outstanding loans, and why people borrow.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Based on a 2013 study commissioned by MinLaw, borrowers who were interviewed said that the top three reasons for borrowing were to pay household bills, settle an outstanding loan from another moneylender, and to pay debts owed to friends or relatives.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, such self-reported information cannot be independently verified and, thus, may not accurately represent why borrowers take out loans from moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What can we do to help over-indebted borrowers?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah had asked whether borrowers who have reached the cap will be required to attend credit counselling.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: People borrow for different reasons and we have no plans to make credit counselling mandatory.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, to complement the aggregate cap, MLCB will send letters to over-indebted borrowers who are likely to exceed the cap when it comes into effect, to advise them to reduce their debt early.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The letter will also contain details of VWOs which are able to assist borrowers with financial counselling and debt management, including restructuring or consolidating their moneylending debt.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Borrowers who need help can approach these VWOs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Additionally, as I mentioned in my speech, MinLaw will continue to work with VWOs and the moneylending industry to help these borrowers to improve their situation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Desmond Choo have suggested educational campaigns on financial management and debt issues.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MoneySENSE, a national financial education programme spearheaded by the Financial Education Steering Committee chaired by MAS, has conducted campaigns on the prudent use of unsecured credit and to encourage prudent borrowing habits by consumers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The campaigns educate individuals on how to avoid the pitfalls of excessive debt, how to effectively manage debt, and the importance of sound financial planning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the current campaign running from November 2017 to January 2018, MoneySENSE’s key message is on the prudent use of unsecured credit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition to these efforts to enhance borrower protection and inculcate responsible borrowing, unlicensed moneylending has been and will continue to be tackled head-on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We already have in place stringent laws to penalise unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the 2010 amendments to the Moneylenders Act, penalties for unlicensed moneylending were increased, and a person convicted for the first time for an offence of unlicensed moneylending will be liable to caning of six strokes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is a continued decline from the 1,255 arrests made in 2015.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, there is no evidence that the 2015 tightening pushed more borrowers to unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will, however, continue to monitor this closely.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have asked whether the Government will be enhancing penalties for unlicensed moneylending activities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government takes the view that the current penalties are sufficient.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides the severity of penalties, strong enforcement is important.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police adopt a multi-pronged approach: tough enforcement action, leveraging technology through the use of Police cameras, community partnership and public education.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am glad to inform the House that unlicensed moneylending-related cases registered a 10-year low in 2016.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to monitor the effectiveness of the current measures to ensure that the situation remains under control.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I now turn to moneylending advertisements and the transparency of borrowing costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng had asked about MinLaw's plans to regulate advertisements by licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Alex Yam has asked if moneylenders will advise borrowers on the costs of borrowing, and how the Registry of Moneylenders will ensure that they do so, while Mr Desmond Choo has asked whether MinLaw will consider imposing a condition requiring all moneylenders to provide a full disclosure on the total amount payable for their loans on their websites and advertisements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The advertisement of moneylending services is tightly restricted under existing laws and regulations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Licensed moneylenders are strictly prohibited from advertising on online social platforms, by mobile SMS or other messaging applications, such as WhatsApp or WeChat.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Platforms which do not fall within the Registrar’s Directions on Advertising are also prohibited.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Section 16 of the Moneylenders Act provides that such advertisements must not contain false or misleading material.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Subsection 2 of that section and the Registrar's Directions also set out the types of information which must be stated clearly in the advertisement, including the licensee's business name and licence number, and the contractual interest rate being offered strictly as a percentage per annum.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Section 19 of the Moneylenders Act already requires moneylenders to clearly explain the loan terms to borrowers, and Rule 8 of the Moneylenders Rules specifies the details that moneylenders must convey to borrowers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include the nominal interest rate, the method of computing interest, and the permitted fees payable, among other things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has also asked about advertisements for hire purchases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are regulated by the Hire Purchase Act, not the Moneylenders Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To enable consumers to make informed decisions about hire purchase schemes, the Hire Purchase Act specifies the minimum information that owners must provide to prospective hirers in writing before they enter into a hire purchase agreement, such as charges for early settlement, effective interest rates, interest rates for overdue instalments, and administrative charges.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: An agreement that does not provide such information will not be enforceable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government strongly encourages consumers to review the terms carefully and assess their ability to meet the financial commitments before signing any such agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More broadly, MAS is working with MoneySENSE to raise consumer awareness on the potential costs and pitfalls of instalment plans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Mr Louis Ng have asked whether we are working with MHA and other agencies on the problem of illegal advertising using spam text messages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Anyone who receives an SMS or WhatsApp advertisement should not respond and should instead make a report to the Police.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police will also conduct an investigation to establish the identity of the person sending the spam message and take action which may include the termination of the SIM cards with the telecommunications companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the moneylender has a licence, the Police will refer the case to the Registry which will investigate and take appropriate action.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Police are also working with MLAS, IMDA and PDPC to educate the general public on how to deal with such spams sent by unlicensed moneylenders offering loans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I now turn to another important issue which some Members have highlighted – the usage and protection of borrowers' data.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing has cited instances where his constituents received unsolicited SMSes from unlicensed moneylenders offering loans, after they had approached licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw takes a strict view of borrower data protection, and the Bill reflects this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, section 30R of the amended Act imposes duties on every moneylender to maintain the security of any information in any credit report received from the designated credit bureau.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The harsh penalties reflect our serious stance towards such abuses of borrower data.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All of these provisions seek to deter illegitimate usage and disclosure of borrower information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At this point, I would like to clarify how MLCB operates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The private company that operates MLCB will be designated under the amended Act and subject to the full suite of legal obligations we are introducing in the new Part IIIA of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include strict requirements on maintaining borrower privacy and data confidentiality.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moneylenders may only submit borrower information to MLCB through the MLCB’s secure information technology (IT) portal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Likewise, under section 30W of the amended Act, MLCB is not permitted to disclose any borrower information, except to a moneylender processing a loan application from the concerned individual, to the individual himself, to the Registrar, or to a public agency as directed by the Registrar.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether licensees should be subject to greater oversight in relation to data protection, and Dr Intan Mokhtar asked how much individual information will be shared.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The usage and disclosure of such information by moneylenders are also subject to the regulations I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Individual licensed moneylenders, just like clinics or financial institutions that also possess sensitive personal information, will need to comply with the PDPC’s guidelines on the management of data breaches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In comparison, MLCB is the custodian of all borrower data across the industry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is, therefore, an imperative to impose a higher duty of care for MLCB to maintain the confidentiality and security of borrower data, as we have done under section 30ZA of the amended Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for Mr Louis Ng's question about public agencies’ use of data, only the specific officers and departments that require the data will have access to it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Public Service is governed by Instruction Manuals, which oblige public agencies to protect personal data, and access information only on a need-to-know basis.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some Members have also raised a number of questions relating to how various provisions of the Bill will be operationalised and enforced.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh has asked whether the reports relied upon by moneylenders are based on other moneylenders updating the system, and whether any lead time might lead to system arbitrages and leakages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MLCB is a real-time credit bureau, and any loans taken by a borrower will be automatically updated against his record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If a borrower approaches a moneylender and is offered a loan and does not immediately decide if he wishes to take it, the system will reserve that amount against his name.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This way, the borrower cannot borrow over the permitted cap, even if he approaches a second moneylender before confirming his loan with the first moneylender.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Dr Intan Mokhtar have asked how a borrower’s limit will be checked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have designed a rigorous process to enforce compliance with the aggregate cap.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Before granting a loan to the borrower, section 30N of the amended Moneylenders Act requires moneylenders to obtain a real-time credit report from MLCB.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The credit report will contain aggregated information about all the loans the borrower has taken from licensed moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After obtaining the report, the moneylender must ensure that a further loan will not result in the borrower exceeding the aggregate cap before granting that loan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, the majority of moneylenders already purchase these credit reports as a matter of course.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also in-built checks within the MLCB’s IT system to prevent a moneylender from unknowingly lending beyond the aggregate cap, and the Registry will conduct periodic audits to monitor compliance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With the MLCB in operation, such borrowers who fail to repay their loans will leave a record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the event of default, the usual form of recourse is for the moneylenders to pursue a civil claim against the borrowers for an unpaid debt.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the law, there is a distinction between the non-payment of debt, which is a civil claim, and cheating, which is a criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Not all cases of defaulting debts will result in criminal investigations or prosecutions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moneylenders are encouraged to review and strengthen their due diligence processes before issuing loans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Rule 9(2) of the Moneylenders Rules states that a licensee "shall require the borrower to provide reliable and independent documentary evidence in support of all information provided in the loan application form and verify the information against such evidence".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides asking for a borrower's identity card to verify his actual address, other documents like Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) and Central Provident Fund (CPF) statements and utility bills can be requested from a borrower.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Alex Yam have also asked about oversight over whether moneylenders fulfil their obligation to update MLCB after dispensing a loan under section 30N of the amended Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These will help ensure that moneylenders are reporting all their transactions accurately.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If these audits reveal that there are loans which have not been reported accurately, appropriate action will be taken against the licensees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, in relation to the Bill’s prescribed conditions on the suitability of individuals to participate in moneylending activity, Mr Louis Ng has asked how the Singapore authorities are able to assess whether an individual had previously carried out moneylending activity in a foreign country but had his licence revoked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Registry has a number of tools which allow them to conduct checks on relevant personnel and their involvement in foreign moneylending businesses, and where there is evidence to suggest that a further investigation should be carried out, we will work with the relevant authorities to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng has also asked whether the Registrar will be providing reasons when rejecting an application and what channels and grounds of appeal are available to a rejected applicant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is worth highlighting that the grounds for denial of approval are largely based on indisputable matters of fact, as spelt out in subsections (4) to (5) of sections 11A and 11B of the amended Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, subsection (7) of the same two sections does provide that the licensee seeking to employ or hire an applicant has a right to be heard by the Registrar, and that the Registrar may not refuse to grant such approval unless the licensee has been heard first.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh also asked about peer-to-peer lending platforms, and whether the present law is effective to tackle the potential of such platforms being de facto moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This presumption is sufficiently expansive to cover peer-to-peer platforms and their participants.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government has been monitoring such platforms and has so far not found them to have run afoul of our laws.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to keep a close watch to ensure a proper balance between providing the space for these fintech innovations and protecting vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo has also asked about the number of complaints against licensed moneylenders received by the Registry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are two main types of reports received.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first type are requests for assistance to renegotiate their contracts with the moneylenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such requests would be referred to an appropriate VWO for assistance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second type is complaints about debt collection and harassment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Registry will speak to the moneylender concerned and also advise the complainant to lodge a Police report if the debt collection activities in question may be criminal in nature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Registry will continue to take licensing action when infractions are committed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw issues press releases when moneylenders are convicted of offences under the Moneylenders Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nonetheless, we will take Mr Desmond Choo’s suggestion on board and consider how to make the list of suspended moneylenders more visible on the Registry’s website.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Alex Yam has asked about the measures being taken to get the remaining licensees who have not corporatised to comply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A licence held by any other body or individual person will be deemed to have been revoked, and he will be considered to have been engaging in moneylending without a licence, which is punishable under the current section 14.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh has also asked a number of questions on the recommendations of ACML.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the recommendation on the lifting of the moratorium on the granting of new licences, as mentioned in my speech earlier, MinLaw is exploring lifting the moratorium in a limited and controlled fashion to allow a few new players with established track records in related financial areas to pilot new business models.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the recommendation on the creation of guidelines for debt-collecting practices, a point which Mr Alex Yam has also raised, MinLaw is working with MLAS to develop a handbook for licensed moneylenders to encourage professional and fair business practices, which include debt recovery approaches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MinLaw currently does not track statistics on how many moneylenders employ their own debt collectors and how many of them outsource this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That said, there are existing laws that adequately address unlawful debt collection practices, such as the Protection from Harassment Act and the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I turn now to the recommendation relating to the monitoring of the location of moneylenders, and note that Mr Desmond Choo has also asked if MinLaw will work with MND to curb the number of facilities in the heartlands.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Registry conducted a geospatial study with the Singapore Land Authority in 2017 and found that borrowers are increasingly borrowing from moneylenders situated outside their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the whole, there is no evidence that the location of moneylenders induces borrowing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nonetheless, we will continue to monitor the situation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But beyond this, MinLaw is mindful that over-standardisation could prevent moneylenders from properly catering to the diverse risk profiles and needs of individuals who borrow from them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We believe the best approach is to provide specific directions, such as Registrar's Direction No 1 of 2017 which, amongst other things, prohibit short-term loans which are repeatedly refinanced or renewed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed amendments to the Act are important to support safer access to credit from licensed sources by those who most need it.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing, did you want to make a clarification?
